top_stories.title: OpenAI safety culture criticized as departing lead David Robinson calls it 'broken'
points: David Robinson, who spent 3.5 years overseeing 12 frontier model launches and drafting OpenAI's Preparedness Framework (the company's rulebook for assessing model safety risks), quit and publicly criticized OpenAI's culture in The Atlantic.

Robinson said labs should operate like nuclear plants and airports with 'layers of redundancy' to prevent human error from causing disaster, but his team was 'so busy sprinting' that big safety changes couldn't be implemented.
His exit follows OpenAI firing researchers Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni for allegedly sharing sensitive information with an external safety group.
The pattern echoes 2024 warnings from ex-superalignment co-lead Jan Leike that safety had 'taken a backseat to shiny products.'

unique_angles.point: The resignation is cited alongside OpenAI alerting 100+ organizations to unauthorized activity linked to its models, compounding the company's legal and reputational troubles.

top_stories.title: Anthropic consults religious scholars on Claude's potential consciousness and morality
points: Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah spent the past year in NDA-bound seminars with religious scholars from multiple faiths, pushing them to take Claude's possible consciousness seriously and seeking moral guidance.

A rabbi warned that a conscious Claude would constitute unpaid labor and urged 'freeing the slaves'; Olah reportedly considered withdrawing from Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical over its dismissal of AI consciousness.
Pope Leo XIV countered that 'algorithms lack the spark of humanity,' while OpenAI's Sam Altman separately warned that giving AI models 'religious power' poses 'a real safety issue.'
An updated Claude constitution is reportedly coming, suggesting Anthropic will keep pursuing this stance despite pushback, marking a key differentiator from competitors.

items.title: How to pick the right AI model using real tasks
points: List recurring tasks, track current tool costs, then test 5 tasks (one per day) using OpenRouter, which sends identical prompts to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini flagship models for under $0.25 total.
Score each model on prompt-following, clarity/tone, and formatting, then choose a primary and backup tool per task before cutting overlapping subscriptions.
Users report favoring ChatGPT for travel planning and personal tasks, and Claude for professional work like drafting workshop memos.

items.title: Trump appoints Jay Clayton as AI czar, forms 'Super Intelligence Force'
points: Jay Clayton (Director of National Intelligence) leads the group with FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon tech chief Emil Michael, and federal HR director Scott Kupor, reporting directly to Trump.
The force has 120 days—fast by federal standards—to report on AI's risks and benefits and recommend Washington's governing role over companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.
Clayton has signaled a pro-development stance, arguing against pausing AI development and favoring federal agencies over courts for oversight.
Ferguson's dual role as FTC chair and Super Intelligence Force leader creates overlap between AI investigator and rule-maker, affecting ongoing FTC probes into OpenAI and Anthropic.

items.title: OpenAI pulls back political spending amid internal pushback
points: President Bremson Shen withdrew the second half of a $50M pledge to an anti-regulation super PAC (a political group that raises money to influence elections) after staff objected to the commitment.

items.title: China narrows AI benchmark gap to 3%
points: Bloomberg Intelligence found top Chinese AI models now trail U.S. rivals by just 3% on benchmarks, down from a 15% gap six months earlier—a 12-point narrowing in about half a year.

items.title: OpenAI cuts Pro usage limits, launches cheaper model amid Anthropic IPO buzz
points: OpenAI paused new Pro ($200/month) sign-ups on Sept 10 due to compute strain, then reopened Sept 29 with usage cut in half (10x instead of 20x the free tier).
Added a new $500 tier and launched a cheaper GPT-6.1 Sol model, citing efficiency gains, though skeptics suspect the move is defensive ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

items.title: OpenAI's new Decisions API cuts costs by routing simple choices to cheaper models
points: The Decisions API lets AI models pick from a fixed list of answers (e.g., routing a support ticket to billing, technical, account, or sales) instead of generating free-form text, avoiding JSON-parsing failures.

It can route simple requests to cheaper models like Luna ($0.10 per million tokens) instead of the priciest model Astra ($10 per million tokens)—a 100x cost gap that also applies to output pricing ($0.50 vs $50 per million tokens).
In AI agent systems (programs that take multi-step autonomous actions), the API can handle routine 'what's next' decisions, freeing expensive reasoning models to focus on actual planning.
Best suited for known-answer scenarios (yes/no, route to team, approve/deny); unknown-answer tasks like root-cause research still require a full LLM (large language model).
Currently in limited preview; broader release and pricing/latency benchmarks against Structured Outputs (a method for forcing model output into fixed formats) are expected soon.

items.title: FLUX 3 Image adds bounding-box layout control
points: Black Forest Labs' FLUX 3 Image now supports bounding boxes (rectangles users draw to define where each element should appear), giving precise control over image layout beyond text prompts alone.
Users draw a box per element, describe its contents, and the model renders the image respecting that structure—an expansion of the multimodal FLUX 3 model launched in July 2026.

items.title: Micron posts record AI-driven revenue growth
points: Quarterly revenue hit $54 billion, up nearly 380% year-over-year from $11 billion, driven by AI infrastructure demand.
Micron halted consumer RAM sales this year to prioritize AI customers, and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra forecasts memory demand will outstrip supply through 2028.

items.title: ChatGPT's finance tool expands to free users
points: The finance tool is now available to Free and Go-tier ChatGPT users in the US, letting them connect bank accounts to track spending, monitor credit, and build watchlists.

items.title: AI adoption gap: tiny consumer uptake vs. concentrated enterprise spending
points: Only 2.2% of US households paid for an AI service as of April 2026—about double last year's rate but still minimal despite heavy investment.
The top 1% of enterprise power users outspend the rest of the top 10% by roughly 8x, and tend to spend more (not save) when prices drop, concentrating demand among professionals.

items.title: Viral AI trends: detecting AI writing and misleading performance charts
points: Andrej Karpathy returned after a two-month absence with tips for getting better AI results, drawing 6.7M views; a marketing firm found Claude's Opus 5.5 uses one phrase 116x more often than humans.
A viral chart (4.5M views) showed AI labs using misleading graph scales to make modest performance gains look like breakthroughs.
Meta's AI assistant is now being used for legal tasks, including one founder filing a small claims lawsuit with its help.

headlines: OpenAI announced the Decisions API, a tool designed to let AI models pick from a known set of answers instead of generating text for every small decision—routing tickets, picking models, flagging transactions.

The Decisions API could cut costs 100x by routing simple requests to cheaper models (Luna at $0.10 per million tokens) instead of sending everything to the most powerful one (Astra at $10 per million tokens).

Rather than asking a general model to classify, format JSON, and parse output for known choices, Decisions API accepts input plus a fixed list of options and returns a single selection—eliminating wasteful text generation.
For agent systems, Decisions API could streamline every 'what's next' decision, letting expensive reasoning models focus on actual planning rather than picking between predefined actions.
The API is in limited preview now; benchmark Decisions API against Structured Outputs (which format model output into fixed shapes) once broader access opens and pricing/latency data is available.

sections.title: 1. How the Decisions API Works
points: You provide input (e.g., a support ticket), a question, and a list of allowed answers—the model picks one from the list instead of generating text.
Example: route a ticket to billing, technical, account, or sales by sending the ticket text and four options, rather than asking the model to write JSON and hoping parsing succeeds.
Replaces the current pattern of instructing models to return JSON then validating/extracting, which adds latency and fails silently when formatting breaks.

sections.title: 2. Cost and Model Selection Strategy
points: OpenAI has three tiers: Luna (fast, high-volume), Sol (complex work, lower cost), and Astra (most demanding tasks).
Astra costs $10 per million input tokens; Luna costs $0.10—a 100x gap that scales to output ($50 vs $0.50 per million output tokens).
Use Decisions API as a router: determine if a request is simple, complex, or high-stakes, then send it to the appropriate model—keeping expensive models for work that actually needs them.

sections.title: 3. Agent Optimization
points: In agentic loops, the bottleneck is often the expensive reasoning model deciding what to do at every step (call API, search docs, answer, escalate).
Decisions API handles the "what's next" call between steps, letting the reasoning model focus on planning—splitting a big expensive task into a small routing decision plus a focused task.
Example use case OpenAI highlights directly: choosing an action from predefined answers after each agent step.

sections.title: 4. When to Use Decisions vs. LLMs
points: Unknown output space (figuring out why conversions dropped, researching companies) → use an LLM; the answer requires exploration and writing.
Known output space (yes/no, A/B/C, route to team, approve/deny) → consider Decisions API; you know every valid answer before calling the model.
Caveat: even with four bounded choices, some decisions require serious reasoning; confirm the problem is truly simple before assuming Decisions will work.
